title: Why the sky and clouds are far away
status: Language review draft — user-supplied Navrongo wording recorded; other composed Kasem sentences remain unverified
attribution: Adapted from the plot supplied by the user. Expanded dialogue and scenes are newly written; this is not a documented traditional Kasem transcription.
variety: Navrongo Kasem, requested by the user. Remaining dictionary-based draft needs adaptation from the Burkina Faso reference variety.

userSuppliedLanguage.kasem: ye ta n zɔ wɛ yuu kom
wɛ maa pa wɛ yuu kom wo baŋa baŋa

userSuppliedLanguage.english: People fetched clouds and cooked with them
userSuppliedLanguage.kasem: nɔɔna maa yeini ba kwoni konkweino tem ye ba mae ba saŋe

panels.caption: Wɛ bwələ.
panels.meaning: Long ago. The sky is near. Storyteller: Here is my story? Listeners: We are listening!
panels.scene: Long, long ago, the land and the sky lived close together. Clouds hung low over the compounds, within reach of an outstretched hand. At dusk, the children gathered to hear how everything had changed.
panels.review: Caption is a new composition: needs past-time wording and an explicit reference to the land. Opening call and response are dictionary-attested, but local storytelling formula and spelling need confirmation.

panels.caption: nɔɔna maa yeini ba kwoni konkweino tem ye ba mae ba saŋe
panels.bubble: [Gather only what we need for cooking.]
panels.meaning: People fetched clouds and cooked with them (exact user-supplied Navrongo sentence). Square brackets mark untranslated dialogue.
panels.scene: When it was time to cook, people lifted their calabashes and fetched pieces of cloud. A little went into each cooking pot. A child reached for one more handful, but an elder smiled: ‘Gather only what we need. There is enough for everyone.’
panels.review: Main caption supplied by the user in Navrongo Kasem; spelling and lowercase preserved exactly. Scene pill konkweino is taken from that sentence; confirm that it works as a standalone label for clouds. Both dialogue bubbles still need translation.

panels.caption: Kazɩm wʋm zɔ sakɔra.
panels.meaning: Old woman. Intended: The old woman pounds fufu. sakɔra is user-supplied; the sentence around it remains provisional.
panels.scene: Then an old witch began pounding fufu in her courtyard. Her pestle was unusually long. Thump into the mortar; knock against the sky. Thump, knock! She frowned at the clouds above her: ‘My fufu must be smooth!’
panels.review: sakɔra is user-supplied Navrongo wording. The full pounding sentence and natural wording for old witch still need Navrongo review. cɩrʋ is a Burkina dictionary candidate for witch.

panels.caption: Baŋa-Wɛ kaanɩ kazɩm wʋm.
panels.reply: ye ta n zɔ wɛ yuu kom
panels.meaning: God. Intended: God warns the old woman. Listen to my words. Stop hitting the sky (user-supplied Navrongo wording).
panels.scene: A voice came from above, calm but clear. ‘Old woman, listen. Lower your pestle. Each time you lift it so high, you strike the sky.’ She paused, glanced upward, and tightened her grip.
panels.review: The exact line ye ta n zɔ wɛ yuu kom was supplied by the user. The warning caption, listen phrase, and name Baŋa-Wɛ still need Navrongo review.

panels.caption: O vɩn Baŋa-Wɛ ni.
panels.bubble: [Please listen. We all cook with these clouds.]
panels.reply: [Let the sky move. I am not finished!]
panels.meaning: Pestle. She refuses to obey God.
panels.scene: But the witch would not listen. Thump, knock! God warned her again. Her neighbors hurried over: ‘Please stop. We all cook with these clouds.’ She waved them away. ‘Let the sky move. I am not finished!’
panels.review: Refusal sentence adapts a dictionary pattern and needs grammar review. Both bubbles need translation, especially the defiant ‘Let the sky move’ construction.

panels.caption: Baŋa-Wɛ daa kaanɩ kazɩm wʋm. O daa magɩ wɛ.
panels.bubble: [If you keep striking the sky, I will raise it beyond your reach.]
panels.meaning: Again. God warns the old woman again. She hits the sky again.
panels.scene: For a third time, God warned her: ‘If you keep striking the sky, I will raise it beyond your reach.’ The courtyard fell quiet. Then she lifted the pestle higher than before. ‘Just one more blow!’ Knock!
panels.review: Both sentences are provisional: verify narrative tense, daa placement and object form of sky. The conditional warning and ‘one more blow’ remain untranslated. Three warnings are an expansion of the user's repeated-warning plot.

panels.caption: wɛ maa pa wɛ yuu kom wo baŋa baŋa
panels.meaning: Upwards. God made the sky rise (exact user-supplied Navrongo sentence). The bubble awaits translation.
panels.scene: God made the sky rise. Up past the roofs, up past the tallest trees, up beyond every reaching hand. The clouds went with it. ‘The clouds!’ cried the child. The witch lowered her pestle at last, but the sky kept rising.
panels.review: Main caption supplied by the user in Navrongo Kasem; spelling and lowercase preserved exactly. Still need taking the clouds with it, the child's exclamation, and local wording for the scene pill.

panels.caption: Wɛ baŋwɔ.
panels.bubble: [Can we ever reach the clouds again?]
panels.reply: [That is why we must listen when we are warned.]
panels.meaning: Nowadays. The sky is far away.
panels.scene: That evening, the pots waited beside the hearth. Nobody could fetch a single cloud. ‘Can we ever reach them again?’ the child asked. The elder looked at the distant sky. ‘That is why we must listen when we are warned.’ And from that day, the sky and the clouds remained far above the land.
panels.review: Caption and proposed short title adapt a dictionary distance pattern; confirm baŋwɛ versus baŋwɔ in context. Closing formula, moral, question, and full ‘from that day’ conclusion still need translation.
